body_html:
Spanish slang is where textbook Spanish meets real life. It is the language of group chats, TV series, soccer games and family parties, and it changes from country to country far more than grammar does. A friend in Mexico City says ¡qué chido!, a friend in Madrid says ¡qué guay!, one in Buenos Aires says ¡qué copado! and one in Medellín says ¡qué bacano!, and they all mean “how cool!”. In my translation work, slang is where I spend the most time checking, because a word that is friendly in one country can be rude in another. This guide brings it all together: slang by country, idioms and sayings, filler words and the words to avoid, with a full guide and a quiz for each.

Key takeaways
  • Spanish slang is regional: learn the slang of the country you deal with most.
  • Some words are friendly in one country and offensive in another, such as coger.
  • Idioms and proverbs are shared more widely than slang, and they are safer to use.
  • Filler words like pues, este and o sea make you sound natural faster than any slang word.
  • Recognize vulgar words; don’t rush to use them.
{{toc}}

Why learn Spanish slang?

You can speak correct Spanish for years and still feel lost in a casual conversation. That gap is mostly slang, idioms and the small words that fill real speech. Learning a little of it helps in three ways.

  • You understand more. TV series, music, social media and family chats are full of slang. Knowing neta or parce turns confusion into a laugh.
  • You sound warmer. One well-placed ¡qué padre! at the right moment shows people you are paying attention to how they really talk.
  • You avoid embarrassing mistakes. Knowing which words are vulgar in which country protects you more than any grammar rule.

There is also a limit. Slang belongs in casual settings, with people who use it with you. In emails, job interviews and with your partner’s grandparents, standard Spanish is the better choice; see {{link:writing-emails-in-spanish|writing emails in Spanish}} and {{link:tu-vs-usted|tú vs usted}}.

Slang, idioms and dichos: what’s the difference?

These words get mixed up, so it helps to separate them:

  • Slang (jerga, or in Mexico caló for older street slang) is informal vocabulary, usually regional and often generational: chido, guay, parce.
  • Idioms (modismos or expresiones idiomáticas) are fixed phrases whose meaning isn’t the sum of their words: tomar el pelo (to pull someone’s leg).
  • Proverbs (refranes, or dichos in Mexico) are traditional sayings that give advice: más vale tarde que nunca.
  • Filler words (muletillas) are small words that keep speech flowing: pues, este, o sea.

Slang is the most regional and the riskiest; proverbs are the most widely shared and the safest. That is why this guide moves from slang to idioms to fillers, and why I suggest learners collect them in the opposite order.

Spanish slang by country

Each country, and often each city, has its own slang. Below are the essentials for the four varieties learners in the United States meet most, followed by a quick look at others.

Mexico

Mexican slang is the variety you are most likely to hear in the United States. It is playful, full of nicknames and very sensitive to context: the same word can be friendly with a buddy and rude with a stranger.

  • ¿Qué onda?: what’s up?
  • güey: dude (friends only)
  • chido / padre: cool
  • ¿neta?: really?
  • no manches: no way!
  • lana: money
  • chamba: job
  • ¿mande?: sorry? / yes? (polite)

A word to watch is ahorita: it literally means “right now”, but it can mean anything from “in a minute” to “later today”. Understanding that is as much culture as vocabulary. Full guide with examples and a quiz: {{link:mexican-slang|Mexican slang}}.

Spain

Spanish slang from Spain sounds very different from Latin American slang. Expect vale in every sentence, tío and tía for friends, and strong words that are casual among friends but still rude.

  • vale: okay
  • tío / tía: dude, guy / girl
  • guay / mola: cool / I like it
  • flipar: to be amazed
  • currar: to work
  • pasta: money
  • quedar: to meet up
  • estar hecho polvo: to be exhausted

Spaniards also use vosotros for “you all”, so slang often comes in that form: ¿Qué hacéis, tíos? (What are you guys up to?). In Latin America, the same question would be ¿Qué hacen? Full guide: {{link:spain-slang|Spain slang}}.

Argentina

Argentine slang mixes lunfardo, the old slang of Buenos Aires, with voseo, the use of vos instead of tú. It is instantly recognizable and very expressive.

  • che: hey
  • dale: okay, sure
  • bárbaro / copado: great / cool
  • re: very
  • laburo: job
  • guita: money
  • quilombo: mess
  • boludo: dude, or idiot (careful)

Voseo changes the verbs too: vos sos, vos tenés, vení, mirá. Once you hear it, Argentine slang becomes much easier to follow, and the famous sh sound for ll and y gives it away immediately. Full guide: {{link:argentine-slang|Argentine slang}}.

Colombia

Colombian slang is famous for being friendly and polite at the same time. Many Colombians use usted even with friends, and apologize with qué pena.

  • parce: buddy
  • bacano / chévere: cool, great
  • ¿qué más?: how are you?
  • de una: sure, right away
  • qué pena: sorry, excuse me
  • tinto: black coffee
  • guayabo: hangover
  • plata: money

Colombians also ask for things with ¿me regala…? (literally “will you gift me…?”), even when paying, and offer with ¿le provoca…? (would you like…?). It is a good example of slang that is really politeness. Full guide: {{link:colombian-slang|Colombian slang}}.

Other countries at a glance

  • Chile: ¿cachai? (get it?), po (a filler from pues: sí, po), fome (boring), pololo and polola (boyfriend and girlfriend).
  • Puerto Rico: ¡wepa! (yay!), janguear (to hang out), chavos (money), brutal (awesome).
  • Venezuela: chamo and chama (kid, guy, girl), pana (buddy), chévere (great), burda (a lot).
  • Cuba and the Dominican Republic: asere (buddy, Cuba), ¿qué lo que? (what’s up?, Dominican Republic), vaina (thing, stuff), chévere (great).
  • Peru: pata (buddy), chamba (work), jato (home), bacán (cool).

Thanks to TV, music and social media, most Spanish speakers recognize the main words from other countries. But using the local version is what makes you sound natural. I write more about these broader differences in {{link:latin-american-vs-spain-spanish|Latin American vs Spain Spanish}}.

Spanish slang in the United States

Spanish in the United States has developed slang of its own, shaped by daily contact with English. Many words borrow from English and give it Spanish endings: parquear (to park), la troca (the truck), el lonche (lunch), textear (to text) and la marqueta (the market) are common in Mexican-American communities, especially in the Southwest. Some come from older Chicano and pachuco slang, such as ese (dude) and ándale (come on, hurry).

These words are a natural part of bilingual life, and they say a lot about where someone grew up. They are less useful if you travel to Mexico City or Madrid, where people may not use them. If you hear them from family or coworkers, enjoy them; if you are writing formally, use the standard words: estacionar, la camioneta, el almuerzo, mandar un mensaje. For more on mixing the two languages, see {{link:code-switching-english-spanish|code-switching between English and Spanish}} and {{link:heritage-spanish-speakers|heritage Spanish speakers}}.

Reacting like a native: surprise, agreement and annoyance

Slang is most useful in reactions, the short words that show you are following a conversation. Here are the most common ones, by feeling:

FeelingMexicoSpainArgentinaColombia
Surprise¡No manches!¡Flipo!¡No te puedo creer!¡Uy, no!
Agreement¡Órale!¡Vale!¡Dale!¡De una!
Annoyance¡Qué gacho!¡Qué rollo!¡Qué bajón!¡Qué mamera!
Excitement¡Qué padre!¡Qué guay!¡Bárbaro!¡Qué bacano!

Learning just the row for the country you care about gives you four reactions you can use every day.

One conversation, two countries

To see how much slang changes, here is the same short chat between friends in Mexico and in Spain.

Mexico: —¿Qué onda, güey? ¿Vamos por unas chelas? —Órale, pero no traigo lana. —No hay pedo, yo invito.

Spain: —¿Qué pasa, tío? ¿Nos tomamos unas cañas? —Vale, pero no tengo pasta. —Tranqui, invito yo.

Both mean: “What’s up, dude? Shall we grab a few beers?” “Sure, but I don’t have any money.” “No problem, it’s on me.” Notice that no hay pedo (no problem) is casual and a little vulgar in Mexico; no hay problema works everywhere.

Slang changes fast

Slang has a short life. Words that sounded cool to one generation can sound dated to the next, and social media speeds this up: expressions spread from a TikTok video in Mexico City to teenagers in Los Angeles within weeks. Older words like chido and guay have lasted for decades, but newer ones come and go. When in doubt, listen to people your own age and copy what they say, not what a list from years ago says.

Idioms and sayings

Idioms and proverbs travel much better than slang. A saying like más vale tarde que nunca is understood from Mexico to Spain, and many idioms are shared across the whole Spanish-speaking world. They are also safer to use, because they are rarely rude.

Spanish proverbs

Proverbs, called refranes or, in Mexico, dichos, are a big part of family conversation. Al que madruga, Dios lo ayuda (the early bird catches the worm), camarón que se duerme se lo lleva la corriente (snooze and you lose) and dime con quién andas y te diré quién eres (you are the company you keep) are among the most common. Full guide: {{link:spanish-proverbs|Spanish proverbs}}.

English idioms in Spanish

English idioms almost never translate word for word. A piece of cake is pan comido, it’s raining cats and dogs is llueve a cántaros and to pull someone’s leg is tomar el pelo. Full guide: {{link:english-idioms-in-spanish|English idioms in Spanish}}.

Animal idioms

Spanish loves animal expressions: ser un gallina (to be a coward), estar como pez en el agua (to be in your element), aquí hay gato encerrado (something fishy is going on). Full guide: {{link:spanish-animal-idioms|Spanish animal idioms}}.

Filler words: the fastest way to sound natural

If you only learn one thing from this guide, make it filler words. Replacing English “um” with este… (Mexico) or eh…, starting sentences with bueno or pues, and explaining with o sea or es que will make you sound more natural than any slang word, and none of them are risky. Full guide: {{link:spanish-filler-words|Spanish filler words}}.

{{book:the-mind-lies}}

Words to be careful with

Some of the most common Spanish slang words are vulgar, and some harmless words in one country are rude in another. A few that cause real trouble:

WordWhere it’s fineWhere it’s a problem
cogerSpain: to take, to catchMexico, Argentina and much of Latin America: vulgar
conchaMost countries: shellArgentina, Uruguay: vulgar
güey, boludoBetween close friendsWith strangers, older people or at work: rude
¡hostia!, ¡joder!Very common among friends in SpainStill swear words; avoid in formal settings
¡qué chimba!Medellín, among friends: awesomeVulgar origin; rude in other contexts

For other classic traps, such as embarazada and estoy caliente, see {{link:embarrassing-spanish-mistakes|embarrassing Spanish mistakes}}.

Slang in texting and social media

Much of today’s Spanish slang lives in messages: jajaja for laughter, tqm for te quiero mucho, xq for porque and regional words mixed with emojis. Writing slang is also where spelling gets creative, so you will see wey for güey and k for que. My guide to {{link:texting-in-spanish|texting in Spanish}} covers abbreviations and tone, and {{link:code-switching-english-spanish|code-switching between English and Spanish}} explains why bilingual speakers mix the two so naturally.

What translating slang has taught me

Slang is the part of translation where a dictionary helps least. A word like padre means “father” in every dictionary, but in Mexico ¡qué padre! means “how cool!”. Qué pena means “what a pity” in most countries, but in Colombia it usually means “sorry”. When I translate dialogue, I always ask two questions: which country is the speaker from, and how close are the people talking? The answer changes the right word completely.

The same questions work for learners. Before you use a slang word, ask yourself where you heard it, who said it, and to whom. If a friend from Monterrey uses güey with you, you can use it back. If you only heard it in a movie, wait. For checking regional meanings, the Spanish language academies publish the Diccionario de americanismos, which labels words by country and register.

{{image:3}}

How to learn Spanish slang safely

  1. Choose one country. Learn the slang of the people you talk to most. For most learners in the United States, that is Mexico.
  2. Start with friendly words. ¿Qué onda?, chido, ¡órale! and de una are safe almost anywhere they are used.
  3. Learn in context. Note the whole sentence and who said it, not just the word. See {{link:sentence-mining-spanish|sentence mining}}.
  4. Recognize before you use. Vulgar and strong words are worth understanding, not repeating.
  5. Follow the other person’s lead. If they use slang with you, you can use it back.

Final thoughts

Spanish slang is not a shortcut around learning Spanish; it is the last layer that makes everything else sound real. Start with filler words, add a handful of friendly slang from the country you care about, learn a few proverbs, and keep the strong words for recognition only. Pick one guide above and take its quiz today.

faq.q: What is the most common Spanish slang word?
faq.a: It depends on the country. In Mexico, güey and qué onda; in Spain, vale and tío; in Argentina, che and boludo; in Colombia, parce and qué más.

faq.q: Is Spanish slang the same in every country?
faq.a: No. Slang is very regional. Idioms and proverbs are shared much more widely.

faq.q: Which Spanish slang should I learn first?
faq.a: Learn the slang of the country you deal with most. In the United States, that is usually Mexican slang.

faq.q: Is it rude to use slang in Spanish?
faq.a: Friendly slang with friends is fine. Some words are vulgar or insulting, and a few are harmless in one country but rude in another.

faq.q: How do you say “cool” in Spanish slang?
faq.a: Chido or padre in Mexico, guay in Spain, copado in Argentina and bacano in Colombia.

faq.q: Do I need slang to speak Spanish well?
faq.a: Not to be understood, but it helps you understand real conversations and sound more natural.
